name: Porto
tagline: Granite, port wine and the river Douro's working banks.
bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep and Oct
whenBlurb: Late spring and early autumn are warm and dry, with São João's midsummer madness on June 23rd; winters are wet and summers busy.

ourTake.lede: Porto is smaller and moodier than Lisbon, and better for it: the pleasure here is the river, the granite streets and the port lodges across the water in Gaia. Do one serious cellar visit and a tasting rather than three, walk the Ribeira at golden hour, and don't over-schedule; the city is compact enough to be enjoyed by drifting. The Douro valley is the reward for an extra day or two.
ourTake.comeIf: You love port cellars, riverside tiles and unhurried food-and-wine days.
ourTake.skipIf: You want beaches, big-ticket sights or a fast-moving metropolis.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: The Yeatman
items.area: Vila Nova de Gaia (across the Douro)
credentials: Home to The Yeatman restaurant, MICHELIN ★★ (2026)
items.description: Porto's defining luxury address, a wine hotel terraced into the Gaia hillside, every room facing the old city and the river below.

items.name: Maison Albar, Le Monumental Palace
items.description: A restored Belle Époque palace on the grand avenue, Parisian glamour and marble, in the ceremonial heart of the city.

items.name: Pestana Palácio do Freixo
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
Palácio do Freixo, a classified National Monument (1910)
items.description: A UNESCO-listed baroque palace by Nasoni on the banks of the Douro, a national monument turned pousada, with gardens to the water.

items.name: Vila Foz Hotel & Spa
credentials: Home to Vila Foz restaurant, MICHELIN ★ (2026)
items.description: A 19th-century mansion on the ocean edge, reimagined by designer Nini Andrade Silva, sea, spa and a starred table where the Douro meets the Atlantic.

items.name: Torel Avantgarde
items.description: A design-led house tumbling down the hill toward the river, art-forward rooms, each themed to an artist, with some of the best views in the old town.

items.name: Torel Palace Porto
items.description: Two restored 19th-century palacetes near the Casa da Música, quiet grandeur, a garden and a pool, a step back from the tourist core.

items.name: GA Palace Hotel & Spa
items.description: A restored 19th-century villa near the river's mouth, a small, polished house with a spa and a considered, contemporary hand.

items.name: Torel 1884
items.description: A boutique house on a Ribeira square themed to the great Age of Discoveries, richly detailed rooms steps from the riverfront.

items.name: PortoBay Flores
items.description: A restored 16th-century palace on Porto's prettiest shopping street, a heritage courtyard hotel in the centre of the old town.

items.name: The Ribeira & Cais da Ribeira riverfront
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Oporto, Luiz I Bridge and Monastery of Serra do Pilar
items.description: Porto's soul: a tumble of medieval houses in ochre, terracotta and blue stacked above the Douro, with the arcaded quay below full of cafes and river light. Walk it in the late afternoon when the sun turns the far bank gold, then have a private guide unpick the two-thousand-year history behind the facades. The heart of the UNESCO-listed old town.

items.name: Dom Luís I Bridge
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Oporto, Luiz I Bridge and Monastery of Serra do Pilar
items.description: The double-deck iron bridge (1881-86) that frames every postcard of Porto, linking the old town to the port lodges across the river. Walk the upper deck alongside the metro for the finest view in the city, the whole Ribeira falling to the water on one side, Gaia's cellars on the other. Best at dusk when both banks light up.

items.name: Monastery of Serra do Pilar
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Oporto, Luiz I Bridge and Monastery of Serra do Pilar
items.description: The circular 16th-century church and cloister crowning the Gaia hilltop, and the single best viewpoint over Porto, the Dom Luís I bridge and the river bend. Reached in a moment from the bridge's upper deck; go at golden hour for the panorama, then let a guide explain its role in the siege of Porto.

items.name: Taylor's Port cellars
items.description: One of the oldest port houses (founded 1692) and still independently family-run, with historic lodges, a beautiful audio-guided cellar walk and a hilltop terrace looking back at Porto. The tawny flight and the Barão Fladgate restaurant reward an unhurried afternoon; easy to arrange a private tasting for a small group.

items.name: Graham's Port lodge
items.description: The most polished of the lodge experiences, high on the hill above Gaia since 1890, with cellars of some 3,000 casks and vintage bottles back to the 1890s. The private vintage tastings and the acclaimed Vinum restaurant, with sweeping river views, suit a discreet, high-end afternoon for a couple or family.

items.name: Sandeman cellars
items.description: The house of the black-caped Don, right on the Gaia riverfront and the liveliest of the big-name tours, its guides in the famous cape. A good, accessible introduction to how port is made and aged; combine the classic tawny and vintage tastings for a first port lesson before moving to the smaller houses.

items.name: WOW, World of Wine cultural district
items.description: A whole hilltop quarter of museums, restaurants and shops carved from converted port cellars, wine and cork museums, a chocolate story, a fashion collection, with terraces over the river. Genuinely multi-generational: children and teenagers have as much to do as the adults, and there are veg-friendly restaurants throughout.

items.name: Ferreira Port lodge
items.description: The great Portuguese-owned house, tied to the legendary Dona Antónia Ferreira who shaped the Douro in the 19th century. A quieter, more historically rich tasting than the tourist-heavy lodges, with a strong story to tell, an elegant stop for those who want depth over spectacle.

items.name: Six Bridges Douro river cruise
items.description: A 50-minute sail in a traditional rabelo boat from the Ribeira quay, gliding under all six bridges that span the river, Dom Luís I, Arrábida, Maria Pia, Infante, São João and Freixo. For an unhurried version, charter a private boat or yacht for sunset with champagne rather than the shared hourly departures.

items.name: Livraria Lello
items.description: The 1906 neo-Gothic bookshop with a scarlet swooping staircase and stained-glass skylight, often called the most beautiful in the world and a muse for Harry Potter lore. Timed tickets are essential and the crowds are real; a private out-of-hours slot, arranged ahead, lets you take it in calm. A short walk from Clérigos.

items.name: Clérigos Tower & church
items.description: Nicolau Nasoni's baroque masterpiece, a 75m granite bell tower visible from across the city. Climb the 225 steps for a 360-degree view over the terracotta roofs to the river; late-evening openings let you see Porto lit at night. The linked church and the Passeio dos Clérigos below are worth the pause.

items.name: São Bento railway station azulejos
items.description: A working train station whose entrance hall is lined with some 20,000 blue-and-white azulejo tiles depicting Portugal's history, battles, royal weddings, the coming of the railway. Free to walk in; ten minutes with a guide turns a photo stop into a lesson in the country's founding myths. Steps from the cathedral and Lello.

items.name: Porto Cathedral (Sé)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Oporto, Luiz I Bridge and Monastery of Serra do Pilar
items.description: The fortress-like Romanesque cathedral on the hill above the old town, with a Gothic cloister of blue-and-white tiles and a silver altarpiece. The terrace out front is one of the great free viewpoints over the river and the Gaia lodges. A cornerstone of the UNESCO historic centre.

items.name: Palácio da Bolsa & the Arab Room
items.description: The 19th-century Stock Exchange Palace built on the old St Francis convent, its show-stopper the Moorish-revival Arab Room modelled on the Alhambra and finished with some 18 kilos of gold. Visits are by guided tour only; a private tour for a small group is the discreet way to see the state rooms without the queue.

items.name: Church of São Francisco
items.description: Behind a plain Gothic shell lies Porto's most astonishing interior, nearly every surface carved and gilded in some 400kg of Brazilian gold, a riot of baroque wood. The eerie catacombs below add a second, sombre note. Small and easy to overwhelm, so go early; a short, unforgettable stop beside the Bolsa.

items.name: Igreja do Carmo azulejo facade
items.description: The 18th-century church whose whole side wall is a vast blue-and-white tile panel (added 1912) showing the founding of the Carmelite order. Next to it stands one of the narrowest houses in the world, squeezed between Carmo and Carmelitas. A five-minute photo and history stop near Lello.

items.name: Capela das Almas (Chapel of Souls)
items.description: A small chapel on the corner of the main shopping street entirely sheathed in some 15,000 blue-and-white tiles depicting the lives of St Francis and St Catherine, a wall of azulejos hiding in plain sight amid the shops. A quick, rewarding detour beside the Bolhão market.

items.name: Crystal Palace Gardens (Jardins do Palácio de Cristal)
items.description: Romantic terraced gardens above the Douro with rose beds, fountains, resident peacocks and one of the finest free views over the river and Gaia. A calm green escape from the old-town crowds; lovely for a slow morning walk or a picnic with a private guide who knows the quiet corners.

items.name: Serralves, museum, villa & park
items.description: Portugal's leading contemporary-art institution: Álvaro Siza's white minimalist museum, the pink Art Deco Serralves Villa, and 18 hectares of gardens and woodland with a treetop walkway. A cultured half-day for families, art for the adults, the park and treetop trail for children. Veg-friendly cafe on site.

items.name: Casa da Música
items.description: Rem Koolhaas's bold, faceted concert hall, a landmark of modern architecture and Porto's finest room for classical, jazz and fado. Take the guided architecture tour by day, or, better, book seats for an evening concert; a striking contrast to the baroque old town.

items.name: Foz do Douro seafront
items.description: Where the river meets the Atlantic, a genteel seaside district of villas, the Pergola da Foz promenade, lighthouses and rock pools. Drive or walk the coastal road at sunset and dine at one of the smart seafood restaurants; the most relaxed, moneyed corner of Porto, away from the tour crowds.

items.name: Mercado do Bolhão
items.description: Porto's grand covered market, trading since 1839 and reopened after a careful restoration, two tiers of iron galleries around an open courtyard, full of flowers, cheese, cured meats, produce and tascas. A vivid sense of daily Porto; go with a guide for tastings and the best stalls, veg options included.

items.name: Rua de Santa Catarina & Café Majestic
items.description: Porto's main pedestrian shopping street, and on it the Majestic, a 1921 Belle Époque cafe of mirrors, carved wood and Art Nouveau flourish, all leather and marble. Take morning coffee and a pastel de nata in its gilded room, then browse the boutiques. Reserve ahead; it is deservedly busy.

items.name: Miragaia quarter
items.description: The old riverside neighbourhood just west of the Ribeira, quieter and more lived-in, laundry on balconies, tiny squares, locals about their day. A rewarding wander for those who have seen the headline sights and want the real, unpolished Porto; lovely on a private walking tour at a slow pace.

items.name: Jardim do Morro
items.description: A small hillside garden at the Gaia end of the upper bridge deck, and the classic sunset perch, the Douro turning to gold below and Porto's roofs glowing across the water. Arrive early evening; pair it with a walk down to the port lodges afterwards.

items.name: Igreja de Santo Ildefonso
items.description: The twin-towered 18th-century church at the top of Santa Catarina, its whole facade wrapped in a huge blue-and-white tile panel from 1932. One of the city's great azulejo set-pieces, and an easy stop between the Majestic cafe and the Bolhão market.

items.name: Miradouro da Vitória
items.description: A tucked-away terrace in the old Jewish quarter with a sweeping, crowd-free view across the tiled roofs to the cathedral and the river. Locals' favourite for a quiet sundowner; a short climb rewards you with the view everyone else queues for elsewhere.

items.name: Funicular dos Guindais
items.description: A short, steep funicular that spares you the climb between the riverside Ribeira and the upper town near the bridge, with fine views of the Douro on the way up. A charming, practical ride that doubles as a viewpoint, useful with children or older travellers.

items.name: Igreja de Santa Clara
items.description: A modest Gothic exterior hiding one of the most lavish gilded baroque interiors in Portugal, recently restored to full glory. Far less visited than São Francisco and all the more rewarding for it, a quiet, dazzling stop near the old city walls.

items.name: Douro Valley wine day-trip (Pinhão & the quintas)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Alto Douro Wine Region
items.description: The world's oldest demarcated wine region and one of the most beautiful, river-carved terraces of vines climbing impossibly steep slopes to Pinhão. Do it privately: two or three great quintas (Quinta do Crasto, Quinta do Noval, Quinta da Pacheca) for tastings and lunch, and a rabelo cruise from Pinhão. Veg lunches on request.

items.name: Quinta do Noval
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Alto Douro Wine Region
items.description: One of the Douro's most storied estates, source of the legendary Nacional vintage ports, with a beautiful terraced vineyard above the Pinhão river. A private visit and vertical tasting here is a pilgrimage for serious port lovers, arrange ahead through the estate.

items.name: Pinhão village & railway station
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Alto Douro Wine Region
items.description: The pretty heart of the Douro wine country, its tiny station famous for azulejo panels of the harvest and river life. The jumping-off point for quinta visits and rabelo cruises; a scenic train from Porto hugs the river the whole way for those who prefer the rails to the road.

items.name: Guimarães day-trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Guimarães
items.description: The birthplace of Portugal and of its first king, Afonso Henriques, a beautifully preserved medieval old town of cobbled lanes and squares, crowned by a 10th-century castle and the Dukes' Palace. Under an hour from Porto; an easy, atmospheric half-day, ideally with a private guide for the history.

items.name: Braga & Bom Jesus do Monte day-trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Sanctuary of Bom Jesus do Monte, Braga
items.description: Portugal's religious capital, with its ancient cathedral and grand baroque churches, and just outside it the sanctuary of Bom Jesus do Monte, a theatrical zig-zag baroque stairway of 573 steps climbing to the church, with a water-powered funicular for those who would rather ride. Often paired with Guimarães in one day.

items.name: Aveiro day-trip
items.description: The 'Portuguese Venice', an hour south, a lagoon town of canals plied by colourful moliceiro boats, Art Nouveau facades and salt pans. Add the striped fishermen's houses of nearby Costa Nova for the photographs. A gentle, pretty contrast to Porto's granite intensity.

items.name: Igreja dos Grilos & the old city walls
items.description: A handsome Mannerist church beside the cathedral hill, with a surviving stretch of Porto's medieval Fernandine walls nearby offering river views. A quieter counterpoint to the crowded Sé terrace for those exploring the upper old town on foot.

items.name: Rua das Flores & the artisan quarter
items.description: The elegant pedestrian street linking São Bento to the river, lined with restored merchant houses, boutique jewellers, specialty coffee and small galleries. The most refined browsing street in the old town; slot it between the station azulejos and the Bolsa.

items.name: Casa do Infante
items.description: A medieval customs house on the riverfront, said to be the birthplace of Henry the Navigator, now a small museum over Roman mosaics uncovered beneath. A compact, worthwhile stop for the history behind Porto's age-of-discoveries wealth, moments from the São Francisco church.

items.name: Palácio das Cardosas & Avenida dos Aliados
items.description: Porto's grand civic boulevard, a sweep of Beaux-Arts facades rising to the ornate City Hall, with the Cardosas palace (now a luxury hotel) anchoring the lower end by São Bento. The city's most monumental space; walk it at night when the buildings are lit.

items.name: Fundação de Serralves Treetop Walk
items.description: A raised timber walkway threading through the crowns of the Serralves park's oldest trees, with viewpoints over the gardens and villa. A gentle, novel highlight for children and grandparents alike within the wider Serralves visit.

items.name: Praia da Luz & the coastal beaches
items.description: Porto's own city beaches strung along the Atlantic promenade at Foz, Praia da Luz, Praia dos Ingleses, with beach-club cafes and sunset bars on the rocks. A relaxed afternoon of sea air after the old-town sightseeing; the water is bracing, the terraces are the draw.

items.name: Vintage tram & the tram museum
items.description: Line 1's restored wooden tram trundles along the river from the Ribeira out to Foz, a slow, scenic ride past the water, ending near the Electric Tram Museum in an old power station. A characterful way to reach the coast, and a treat for children and rail enthusiasts.

items.name: Palacete Pinto Leite / Casa da Companhia gardens
items.description: Restored 19th-century merchant mansions and their gardens now open as boutique venues and tea rooms in the elegant Boavista and Cedofeita districts, a glimpse of the gilded-age Porto that port wealth built. A refined, low-key stop between Serralves and the centre.

items.name: Bolsa do Café / specialty coffee & pastelaria trail
items.description: Porto takes its coffee and cakes seriously, from the historic cafes to the wave of specialty roasters around Rua das Flores and Cedofeita. A morning tasting trail of pastéis de nata, francesinha (in a veg version too) and single-origin coffee, easily arranged with a food guide.

items.name: Igreja de São Lourenço (dos Grilos) viewpoint & Passeio das Virtudes
items.description: A grassy garden terrace tumbling down the hillside above Miragaia, beloved by locals for picnics and one of the finest sunset spots facing west over the river mouth. Uncrowded and unhurried, bring a bottle of Douro white and watch the light go.

items.name: The Yeatman
items.area: Vila Nova de Gaia (across the Douro)
items.description: Ricardo Costa's two-star room high above the river, the region's most celebrated table, matched to one of Portugal's great cellars.

items.name: Casa de Chá da Boa Nova
items.description: Rui Paula's two-star seafood kitchen inside Álvaro Siza's landmark tea house, cooking with the Atlantic breaking on the rocks below.

items.name: Antiqvvm
items.description: Vítor Matos's two-star room in a 19th-century mansion above the Crystal Palace gardens, bold, layered reinterpretations of Portuguese flavour.

items.name: Pedro Lemos
items.description: A long-held star in a stone townhouse near the river's mouth, precise, produce-led cooking and a lovely rooftop terrace.

items.name: Euskalduna Studio
items.description: Vasco Coelho Santos's eight-seat counter facing the open kitchen, the most personal, exacting chef's-counter experience in northern Portugal.

items.name: Le Monument
items.description: Julien Montbabut's star inside the Monumental Palace, French technique and Portuguese produce, in a Belle Époque room on the grand avenue.

items.name: Blind
items.description: Vítor Matos's second Porto star, a playful, contemporary tasting menu that sends the diner into the kitchen's imagination.

items.name: Vinha
items.area: Vila Nova de Gaia (across the Douro)
items.description: Henrique Sá Pessoa's Gaia star, assured contemporary cooking over the river, from one of Portugal's most respected chefs.

items.name: DOP
items.description: Rui Paula's city-centre star, refined, generous Portuguese cooking in a handsome downtown palace of the arts.

items.name: ÉON
items.description: Tiago Bonito's star in a restored palacete, precise, seasonal cooking from one of the north's quiet talents.

items.name: Gastro by Elemento
items.description: Ricardo Dias Ferreira's fire-led star, wood, embers and smoke at the centre of an intense, produce-driven menu.

items.name: IN Diferente
items.description: Angélica Salvador's star near the coast, a personal, contemporary kitchen and one of Porto's newer one-star rooms.

items.name: Cozinha das Flores
items.description: Nuno Mendes's return to Portugal, fire, local produce and tradition, in an intimate room off the old town's prettiest street.

items.name: OMA
items.description: A young, well-travelled team turning out a considered tasting menu at real value, Michelin's pick for quality without ceremony.

items.name: Prova
credentials: A respected Porto wine bar led by sommelier Diogo Amado
items.description: Sommelier Diogo Amado's wine room near the river, some fifty Portuguese wines by the glass, poured with real knowledge.

items.name: Port-lodge tastings, Vila Nova de Gaia
items.area: Vila Nova de Gaia (across the Douro)
credentials: Historic port houses, Graham's, Taylor's, Ferreira and others across the river
items.description: An evening tasting at a historic port house, vintage and tawny flights in the candlelit cellars that made the city famous.

items.name: Aduela
credentials: A landmark of Porto's Baixa bar scene, on the lively Rua das Oliveiras / Rua do Almada
items.description: A cult neighbourhood bar in a former haberdashery, laid-back, characterful and the anchor of Porto's most social drinking street.

items.name: The Royal Cocktail Club
items.description: Porto's most serious cocktail room, velvet, chandeliers and a precise, inventive list; the benchmark for a grown-up drink in the city.

items.name: Base
credentials: A well-known Porto open-air garden bar, in the Cordoaria beside Clérigos
items.description: An open-air garden bar under the pines beside the Clérigos tower, daytime-into-night drinks and DJs in the heart of town.

items.name: Terrace at The Yeatman
items.area: Vila Nova de Gaia (across the Douro)
credentials: Terrace of The Yeatman, MICHELIN One Key hotel, Relais & Châteaux
items.description: A glass of port or a cocktail on the terrace of Porto's grandest hotel, the whole old city and river spread out below.

plan.heading: 3 days in Porto, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.label: Day 1
days.title: The old city and the river

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Livraria Lello at opening, then the Sé and the tiled nave of São Bento station.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Down through Ribeira to the quay, crossing the Dom Luís I bridge on foot to Gaia.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Antiqvvm, Vítor Matos's Michelin room above the Douro.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private tasting and cellar walk at Taylor's, followed by the terrace view over the city.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The trams and gardens of the Foz do Douro, where the river meets the sea.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Grilled fish and vinho verde at Pedro Lemos in the Foz, one star, quiet and precise.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A driver up the Douro to Quinta do Crasto for a vineyard walk and the infinity pool view.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch and tasting at The Yeatman's terrace or a riverside quinta among the terraced vines.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Back in Porto, a nightcap of aged tawny at the Vintage House bar.

items.name: Ribeira
items.description: The postcard riverfront of tiled houses and terraces; atmospheric but busy, best for those who want to be in the middle of it.

items.name: Baixa / Aliados
items.description: The grand civic centre with the best hotels and squares; suits travellers who want polish and everything walkable.

items.name: Cedofeita / Miguel Bombarda
items.description: The arts and galleries quarter, quieter and more local; suits those after independent shops and a slower pace.

events.name: Festa de São João do Porto
events.note: The city's exuberant midsummer festival of bonfires, grilled sardines, plastic hammers and a midnight fireworks display over the river.

events.name: NOS Primavera Sound
events.note: A three-day international indie and electronic festival in the Parque da Cidade, an offshoot of the Barcelona original.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Base yourself in the Ribeira or near the Bolhão; arrange a private tasting at one of the family port houses in Vila Nova de Gaia, and consider a day on the Douro by boat or by the vineyard estates upriver.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport (OPO), a twenty-five-minute drive from the river, with a private car waiting on arrival.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver for the port lodges across the Douro and day trips into the wine valley; the Ribeira and downtown are compact and made for walking.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Coverage is strong across the city; an eSIM activates instantly and wifi is dependable in hotels and lodges.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The euro; cards are universal, cash is rarely needed, and a small rounding-up gesture suffices for tips.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May-June and September deliver warm days and cool Douro evenings; July-August is busy and hot, and the winter months are notably wet, Porto is one of the rainier corners of Iberia.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; connect via a European hub, Lufthansa/SWISS through Frankfurt or Zurich, or Air France via Paris, in business, around 14-16 hours total. TAP Air Portugal or the hub carrier flies the final leg into Porto (OPO); pre-clear Schengen at the European hub and use the Star Alliance lounge there, as Porto's own premium facilities are modest.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No special vaccinations; tap water is potable. Low crime, calm and walkable; standard care with valuables in the Ribeira crowds. No altitude issue.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Straightforward for vegetarians, though the city's tradition is meat-forward; good plant-based spots and some Indian dining exist. Try daTerra (vegetarian buffet) or Essência for refined meat-free plates.
